title: Xiaoxin Li
text:
Xiaoxin Li




Postdoctoral Researcher
Sustainable Photonics Research Center (SPRC)
Hangzhou International Innovation Institute of Beihang University, China
Hangzhou, China

Research Focus
Metasurfaces · Optical Computing · Computational Imaging · Intelligent Optical Sensing


Google Scholar
ResearchGate
GitHub






I am a postdoctoral researcher at the Sustainable Photonics Research Center (SPRC), Hangzhou International Innovation Institute of Beihang University, China. I received my B.S., M.S., and Ph.D. degrees from Harbin Institute of Technology.
My research centers on nanophotonics and metasurface-enabled optical information processing, with particular interests in optical computing, multidimensional computational imaging, structured-light detection, and integrated optical sensing. I develop nanophotonic systems that combine physical optical encoding with computational decoding, aiming to move selected sensing and information-processing functions from conventional electronic back ends into compact optical front ends.

A central theme of my work is the co-design of nanophotonic hardware and computational algorithms—engineering how optical information is encoded, transformed, and detected before it reaches conventional electronic processors.

My research has been published in journals including Nature Communications, ACS Photonics, Advanced Optical Materials, and Advanced Photonics Nexus.

Rather than treating nanophotonics, computing, and imaging as separate topics, my research follows a common framework: engineering the physical transformation of optical information and jointly designing the computational interpretation of the detected signals.






I develop metasurface-based optical processors that implement engineered transformations of optical fields for information processing. My research includes diffractive optical neural networks, optical convolution, task-oriented optical encoding, and multidimensional parallel computing.
A key objective is to exploit the intrinsic parallelism of light to perform selected computational operations directly in the optical domain, reducing the amount of information that must subsequently be processed electronically.








I investigate computational optical sensors that encode multiple dimensions of light before detection, including spectral, polarization, spatial, and depth information.
By co-designing metasurface encoders, image sensors, and reconstruction algorithms, I aim to replace bulky cascaded optical components with compact architectures capable of snapshot and high-dimensional optical sensing. This approach provides a route toward highly integrated imaging systems in which optical hardware and computational inference are designed as a unified sensing pipeline.








I study optical computation under incoherent and broadband illumination, with the goal of extending optical computing from controlled coherent experiments toward practical imaging and machine-vision environments.
My work explores metasurface point-spread functions and optical transfer functions for differentiation, convolution, feature extraction, and task-specific preprocessing. Particular emphasis is placed on architectures compatible with natural scenes, broadband illumination, and conventional image sensors.








I explore the generation, manipulation, and measurement of structured and topologically nontrivial optical fields, including optical vortices, vector beams, hybrid-order Poincaré beams, and optical skyrmions.
My research combines metasurface engineering, diffractive optics, and computational decoding to extract high-dimensional optical information and topological observables with compact optical systems, with potential applications in optical communication, sensing, and photonic information processing.
